content.text: is the cross-validated score of the candidate that won, measured on the same folds that picked it, so it includes the luck that helped it win. Nested cross-validation runs the whole search inside each fold of an outer loop and scores the winner on rows the search never saw. Here
said 0.790, nested CV said 0.765, and new data gave 0.758.
A team has 200 labeled rows and tunes a decision tree with

reads 0.790, so the model card promises 79% accuracy. There's no test set, because 200 rows felt too few to split. On new data, the shipped model gets 0.758. Nothing broke; the 0.790 was never an estimate of the shipped model's accuracy.

items.text: It's a cross-validated score: every candidate was scored only on rows it didn't train on.
The API reference defines it as the mean cross-validated score of the best estimator, which sounds like exactly the number you want to report.
Cross-validation is the method you were told to trust over a single validation split.

content.text: The half-truth: each candidate's cross-validated score is a fair estimate for that candidate, as long as you don't choose among them. The moment the search keeps the maximum of 20 noisy scores, the winner's score is no longer fair: the folds that measured it are the folds that chose it.
A grid search does two jobs with one set of folds: it selects the settings, and it reports how well they did. The second number inherits a bias from the first.
Tuning trains on the validation folds
scikit-learn's grid search guide describes model selection as a way of using the labeled data to "train" the parameters of the grid. The inner folds aren't just measuring the

; they're fitting them. The nested CV example in the scikit-learn gallery says the consequence directly: choosing the parameters that maximize non-nested CV biases the model to the dataset and yields an overly optimistic score. This is the same effect as picking the best of many models on a test set, covered earlier in this path, except that it lives inside

The same example says the size of the effect depends mainly on the size of the dataset and the stability of the model. On iris, with 6 candidates for an SVM, it measures an average gap of 0.0076 between non-nested and nested scores over 30 trials: small. Small datasets, unstable models such as deep trees, and large grids push it up. Cawley and Talbot found that the loss from over-fitting the model selection criterion can be surprisingly large, comparable to the differences between learning algorithms, so it can't be ignored when you compare them.
Nested CV: a search inside each fold

gives each job its own loop. The outer loop splits the data into training and test parts. On each outer training part, the full grid search runs with its own inner folds, picks a setting and refits on that whole part. The outer test part, which the search never touched, scores the result. The average over outer folds estimates the performance of the procedure "tune with this grid, then fit". In scikit-learn it's one line: pass the search object to

from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=5200, n_features=20, n_informative=4,
                           flip_y=0.1, random_state=1)
X_dev, y_dev = X[:200], y[:200]  # the labeled rows you have
X_new, y_new = X[200:], y[200:]  # stands in for production traffic
grid = {"max_depth": range(1, 11), "min_samples_leaf": [1, 10]}
inner = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
search = GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0), grid, cv=inner)
search.fit(X_dev, y_dev)  # 20 candidates x 5 folds
print(f"best_score_ {search.best_score_:.3f}")  # goes into the model card
print(f"new data    {search.score(X_new, y_new):.3f}")
# best_score_ 0.790
# new data    0.758

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, StratifiedKFold, cross_validate
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=5200, n_features=20, n_informative=4,
                           flip_y=0.1, random_state=1)
X_dev, y_dev = X[:200], y[:200]
X_new, y_new = X[200:], y[200:]
grid = {"max_depth": range(1, 11), "min_samples_leaf": [1, 10]}
inner = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
outer = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=1)
search = GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0), grid, cv=inner)
nested = cross_validate(search, X_dev, y_dev, cv=outer, return_estimator=True)
print(f"nested CV {nested['test_score'].mean():.3f}")  # the number to report
print([tuple(s.best_params_.values()) for s in nested["estimator"]])
final = search.fit(X_dev, y_dev)  # the model you ship: all 200 rows
print(f"new data  {final.score(X_new, y_new):.3f}")
# nested CV 0.765
# [(2, 1), (2, 10), (2, 1), (2, 10), (2, 1)]
# new data  0.758

content.text: The 5,000 extra rows play production, something you rarely have.

promised 0.790; new data gave 0.758. Nested CV, using only the 200 development rows, estimated 0.765, within a point. One run proves little, so the same script ran on eight datasets drawn the same way (
overstated new-data accuracy by 2.3 points on average, nested CV by 0.7.
What nested CV gives you, and what it doesn't

It gives you no model and no single best setting. Every outer search here picked a depth of 2, while the search on all 200 rows picked a depth of 4. That's expected: the outer searches see 160 rows each, and their choices tell you how stable the tuning is. The model you ship is the search refit on all the data,
by default, and nested CV is the estimate of how that procedure performs.
The outer scores also show the spread: from 0.60 to 0.875 across the five outer folds. With 40 rows per outer test fold, that's the honest uncertainty of any number you report from 200 rows.

blocks.title: The nested score is honest only once

content.text: If the nested score disappoints and you change the grid, the features or the model family and rerun, the outer folds have started choosing for you, and the next nested score is optimistic too. Make the change, but judge the final choice on data that played no part in it, as scikit-learn's grid search guide recommends: an evaluation set held out from the start.
